domanda: While configuring a policy assignment in the Azure portal, the Remediation tab prompts you to create a managed identity and select a location for it. Which policy effect makes a managed identity mandatory on the assignment?
spiegazione: DeployIfNotExists is correct: policy assignments with the deployIfNotExists effect must have an identity property because Azure Policy executes an ARM template deployment on your behalf, and it authenticates that deployment with a managed identity associated with the assignment. Modify is the only other effect with the same requirement. Audit is wrong because it only assesses the resource's own properties and writes a compliance record - it never changes or deploys anything, so it has no identity to authenticate as. Append is wrong because it alters the request payload before the Resource Provider processes it, inside the policy engine itself; it performs no deployment and therefore explicitly does not require a managed identity (Microsoft recommends Append precisely for cases where you cannot create a managed identity). DenyAction is wrong because it simply blocks a matching action request and, like Deny, takes no action that requires authorization as a separate principal.

domanda: How frequently does Azure Policy automatically re-evaluate already-assigned policies and initiatives as part of the standard compliance evaluation cycle?
spiegazione: Every 24 hours is correct: Microsoft documents the standard compliance evaluation cycle as occurring once every 24 hours, at which point all assignments are automatically re-evaluated and updated compliance results become available in the portal and SDKs. Every 15 minutes is wrong - it confuses the cycle with a different documented figure: when a single resource is created or updated in a scope that has an assignment, the effect event and that individual resource's compliance status appear roughly 15 minutes later, but this does not re-evaluate any other resource. Every hour is wrong; no Azure Policy evaluation trigger is documented on an hourly cadence. Every 7 days is wrong - the seven-day figure relates to the compliance-over-time chart shown on the Policy Overview page, not to the evaluation frequency. If you cannot wait for the cycle, trigger an on-demand scan with Start-AzPolicyComplianceScan or az policy state trigger-scan.

domanda: Contoso has a management group named Corp that contains three subscriptions: Sub1, Sub2, and Sub3. A cloud engineer created a custom policy definition while Sub1 was the selected definition location. You must now assign that same custom definition to all three subscriptions, using the least administrative effort. What should you do?
opzione_a: Assign the existing definition from Sub1 directly to the Corp management group.
opzione_b: Re-create the policy definition using the Corp management group as its definition location, then assign it to Corp.
opzione_c: Export the definition and re-create a separate copy in Sub2 and Sub3, then create three assignments.
opzione_d: Add the existing Sub1 definition to a new initiative in Sub1 and assign the initiative to Corp.
spiegazione: Re-creating the definition at the Corp management group is correct: the definition location determines the scope to which a definition can be assigned, and resources must be within the resource hierarchy of that definition location. A definition stored in a management group can be assigned to that management group and to any child management group or child subscription, so a single definition and a single assignment at Corp covers Sub1, Sub2, and Sub3. Microsoft states explicitly that if you plan to apply a definition to several subscriptions, the definition location must be a management group that contains each subscription. Option A is wrong because a definition whose location is Sub1 can only be assigned within Sub1's hierarchy - the Corp management group is a parent, not a child, so it is outside that hierarchy and the assignment cannot be created. Option C is technically workable but is the opposite of least administrative effort: it produces three definitions and three assignments to keep in sync. Option D is wrong because an initiative inherits the same definition-location constraint; an initiative stored in Sub1 that references a Sub1-scoped definition still cannot be assigned up at the Corp management group.

domanda: Fabrikam requires that every resource in a subscription carry a costCenter tag. Several hundred resources already exist without the tag. You must use Azure Policy to apply the tag to those existing resources and to ensure that resources created in the future receive it automatically. Which effect should the policy definition use?
spiegazione: Modify is correct: it adds, updates, or removes tags on a resource during creation or update, and - critically for this requirement - existing non-compliant resources can be brought into a compliant state through a remediation task, which is supported only for the modify and deployIfNotExists effects. Microsoft explicitly recommends Modify over Append when managing tags, because Modify offers more operation types (addOrReplace, add, remove) and the ability to remediate existing resources. Append is wrong: although it can add a tag on a create or update request, when it runs during an evaluation cycle it makes no changes to resources that already exist - it only marks them non-compliant, and no remediation task can be created for it. Audit is wrong because it only reports the non-compliant resources in the compliance dashboard; it never alters a resource on creation or afterwards. AuditIfNotExists is wrong for the same reason and is additionally the wrong tool here: it assesses a related child or extension resource's properties rather than the tags on the resource itself, and like Audit it cannot remediate.

domanda: An engineer uses Azure CLI to assign a built-in policy definition that has a deployIfNotExists effect, passing --location and --mi-system-assigned so that a system-assigned managed identity is created. The compliance dashboard correctly lists dozens of non-compliant resources, but every deployment started by the remediation task fails with an authorization error. What should you do first to resolve the issue?
opzione_a: Grant the assignment's managed identity the roles listed in the policy definition's roleDefinitionIds property.
opzione_b: Change the assignment's enforcementMode property from DoNotEnforce to Default.
opzione_c: Delete the assignment and re-create it with a user-assigned managed identity instead.
opzione_d: Run Start-AzPolicyComplianceScan against the subscription to refresh the compliance data.
spiegazione: Granting the roles manually is correct. Azure Policy uses the assignment's managed identity to perform the template deployment, and that identity must hold the minimum RBAC roles declared in the definition's roleDefinitionIds. Only the Azure portal grants those roles automatically when the assignment is created; for every other method - Azure CLI, Azure PowerShell, or any SDK - Microsoft states the roles must be granted manually or the remediation deployment will fail. That is exactly the symptom described. Option B is wrong: enforcementMode affects whether the effect fires during resource creation or update, and Microsoft documents that remediation tasks can be started for deployIfNotExists policies even when enforcementMode is DoNotEnforce - it would not produce an authorization error. Option C is wrong because the identity type is irrelevant to the failure: a user-assigned identity created outside the portal needs the same roles granted manually, so re-creating the assignment reproduces the problem. Option D is wrong because compliance evaluation and remediation use different identities - evaluation uses the caller's identity and is clearly working here, since the non-compliant resources are already listed. Re-scanning cannot fix an authorization failure on the deployment.

domanda: Before enforcing a new standard, you assign a policy definition that uses the Deny effect to a production subscription and set the assignment's enforcementMode property to DoNotEnforce. What is the result?
opzione_a: Resources are still evaluated and their compliance state is still reported, but non-compliant create or update requests are not blocked and no Azure Activity log entry is written.
opzione_b: The policy rule is not evaluated at all, so no compliance data is generated for the assignment.
opzione_c: Non-compliant create or update requests are still blocked, but no Azure Activity log entry is written.
opzione_d: Existing non-compliant resources are automatically brought into a compliant state without a remediation task.
spiegazione: Option A is correct. enforcementMode set to DoNotEnforce is the documented 'What If' capability: it lets you test the outcome of a policy on existing resources without initiating the policy effect and without triggering entries in the Azure Activity log. Evaluation still happens, so the compliance dashboard shows you which resources would be affected. Option B is wrong because it describes the Disabled effect, which Microsoft explicitly contrasts with enforcementMode - Disabled prevents resource evaluation from happening at all, whereas DoNotEnforce only suppresses enforcement of the effect. Option C is wrong because it inverts the behaviour: DoNotEnforce is precisely what stops the Deny effect from blocking the request. Option D is wrong on two counts: remediation applies only to deployIfNotExists and modify (never to Deny), and even for those effects existing resources require an explicitly created remediation task - although, notably, such a task can still be started while enforcementMode is DoNotEnforce.

domanda: A custom policy definition uses the append effect with a single field/value pair that targets the non-[*] alias Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/networkAcls.ipRules in order to set an approved IP rule on storage accounts. A developer submits a request to create a storage account whose payload already specifies a different set of values in networkAcls.ipRules. What is the outcome of the request?
opzione_a: The append effect silently overwrites the developer's ipRules with the policy value, and the storage account is created.
opzione_b: The request is rejected, because append behaves as a deny effect when it would override a value in the original request with a different value.
opzione_c: The policy value is added alongside the developer's entries and the storage account is created with the combined array of IP rules.
opzione_d: The storage account is created with the developer's values and is then flagged as non-compliant in the next evaluation cycle.
spiegazione: Option B is correct. Append evaluates before the request is handed to the Resource Provider, and Microsoft documents that if the append effect would override a value in the original request with a different value, then it acts as a deny effect and rejects the request. With a non-[*] alias that maps to an array, append tries to write the value as the entire array, so a pre-existing array causes exactly this conflict and a deny event occurs. Option A is wrong because append never silently overwrites a conflicting value - overwriting behaviour on an existing value is what the modify effect's addOrReplace operation provides, not append. Option C is wrong because it describes the [*] version of the alias: using Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/networkAcls.ipRules[*] appends the value to a potentially pre-existing array (and creates the array if absent). That is the correct authoring fix here, but it is not what the non-[*] alias in this scenario does. Option D is wrong because the request never reaches the Resource Provider - it is rejected up front - so there is no created resource to mark non-compliant.

domanda: You are documenting the difference between excluded scopes (notScopes) on a policy assignment and Azure Policy exemptions for your governance team. Which statements are correct? Each correct answer presents part of the solution. Select all that apply.
opzione_a: Resources within a scope listed in the assignment's notScopes array are not evaluated and are not included in the assignment's compliance count.
opzione_b: A policy exemption is created as a child object on the resource hierarchy or the individual resource that is granted the exemption.
opzione_c: A policy exemption can be made time-bound by setting its expiresOn property.
opzione_d: Adding a scope to notScopes requires creating a Microsoft.Authorization/policyExemptions object at that scope.
opzione_e: Resources covered by a policy exemption are reported in the compliance dashboard with a state of Compliant.
spiegazione: A is correct: exclusion is implemented through the properties.notScopes array on the assignment object, and Microsoft states that resources within these scopes aren't evaluated or included in the compliance count. B is correct: an exemption is a separate Resource Manager object created as a child of the resource hierarchy or individual resource being exempted - which is why deleting the parent resource also removes the exemption. C is correct: the optional expiresOn property (Universal ISO 8601 DateTime) sets when the resource is no longer exempt; note that the object itself is preserved for record-keeping after that date, it just stops being honoured. D is incorrect because it conflates the two features: notScopes is a property of the policy assignment object itself, so excluding a scope means modifying the assignment - no policyExemptions object is involved, and unlike an exemption it requires no exempt/Action permission on the assignment. E is incorrect: the whole point of an exemption over an exclusion is that the resource is still tracked, so it appears with a distinct compliance state of Exempted, not Compliant. Reporting it as Compliant would hide the accepted risk.

domanda: A colleague is authoring a custom policy definition that uses the modify effect and asks you to review the JSON. Which statements about the modify effect are correct? Each correct answer presents part of the solution. Select all that apply.
opzione_a: The Remove operation is supported only for resource tags.
opzione_b: If conflictEffect is not specified, its default value is deny.
opzione_c: During a standard evaluation cycle, modify automatically applies its operations to resources that already exist.
opzione_d: The details property must include a roleDefinitionIds array.
opzione_e: Modify can add or replace the identity.type field on any Azure resource type.
spiegazione: A is correct: of the three supported operations (addOrReplace, add, remove), Microsoft documents that remove is only supported for resource tags - you cannot use it to strip an arbitrary alias-mapped property. B is correct: conflictEffect determines which definition wins when more than one modifies the same property or when the operation does not work on the specified alias, its available values are audit, deny, and disabled, and its default value is deny (Microsoft nonetheless recommends audit for definitions that include aliases, to avoid failing requests on API versions where the property is not Modifiable). D is correct: roleDefinitionIds is a required subproperty of details, and it must contain full role resource IDs, not short role names, because these are the roles the assignment's managed identity needs in order to remediate. C is incorrect - this is the classic misconception. Modify is a skipped modification for existing resources: when it runs as part of an evaluation cycle it makes no changes to resources that already exist, it only marks them non-compliant so they can be remediated through an explicitly created remediation task. E is incorrect: you can only modify identity.type on virtual machines and Virtual Machine Scale Sets. On any other resource type, policy evaluation is skipped altogether and the resource is considered not applicable to the policy.

domanda: Your governance team is planning a large-scale remediation of non-compliant resources across several subscriptions. Which statements about Azure Policy remediation tasks are correct? Each correct answer presents part of the solution. Select all that apply.
opzione_a: Remediation tasks can be created only for assignments whose policy definitions use the deployIfNotExists or modify effect.
opzione_b: When the assignment is created in the Azure portal, Azure Policy can automatically grant the managed identity the roles listed in roleDefinitionIds.
opzione_c: A single remediation task can remediate every deployIfNotExists policy contained in an initiative at the same time.
opzione_d: The location chosen for a system-assigned managed identity determines which regions the remediation task is able to target.
opzione_e: A single remediation task can remediate a maximum of 50,000 resources.
spiegazione: A is correct: Microsoft states that resources non-compliant to policies with deployIfNotExists or modify effects can be put into a compliant state through remediation, and the portal's Policies to remediate tab lists only those two effect types. B is correct: when you create the assignment and its identity through the portal, Azure Policy automatically grants the identity the roles defined in the definition's roleDefinitionIds; for SDK, CLI, or PowerShell the roles must be granted manually. Note the caveat that if roleDefinitionIds are edited later, the new permissions must be granted manually even in the portal. E is correct: the maximum number of resources for a remediation task is 50,000 (the -ResourceCount parameter defaults to 500). C is incorrect: when remediation is initiated from an initiative assignment you must select which policy to remediate from a drop-down, because only one deployIfNotExists or modify policy can be remediated through a single remediation task at a time. D is incorrect: although a location must be specified when a system-assigned identity is created, Microsoft states that the location of the managed identity doesn't affect its operation with Azure Policy. The resources a task targets are filtered by scope and by the optional Locations filter on the task, not by the identity's location.

domanda: Your team is authoring a custom policy definition that uses the deployIfNotExists effect to deploy a diagnostic setting when one is missing, and you are preparing the corresponding assignment. Select the correct answer for each drop-down to complete the design notes. (The definition's details property omits evaluationDelay, existenceScope, and deploymentScope.)
opzione_a: Value used for evaluationDelay: [PT5M | PT10M | PT30M]
opzione_b: Value used for existenceScope: [ResourceGroup | Subscription | ManagementGroup]
opzione_c: Template style supported inside the deployment property: [Linked templates | Nested templates | Both linked and nested templates]
opzione_d: Managed identities that can be associated with the assignment: [One system-assigned or one user-assigned identity | One system-assigned identity and one user-assigned identity | Any number of user-assigned identities]
risposta_corretta: PT10M,ResourceGroup,Nested templates,One system-assigned or one user-assigned identity
spiegazione: evaluationDelay defaults to PT10M (10 minutes): it specifies when the existence of the related resources is evaluated after a create or update request, and accepts AfterProvisioning, AfterProvisioningSuccess, AfterProvisioningFailure, or an ISO 8601 duration between 0 and 360 minutes. PT5M and PT30M are valid values you could set, but neither is the default. existenceScope defaults to ResourceGroup, which limits the query for the related resource to the evaluated resource's resource group; Subscription is a valid alternative that queries the whole subscription (and requires the assignment scope to be at subscription level or higher), but it is not the default, and ManagementGroup is not an allowed value for existenceScope at all. Nested templates are supported with deployIfNotExists, while Microsoft states that linked templates are currently not supported - which rules out both other choices. Finally, a single policy assignment can be associated with only one managed identity, either system-assigned or user-assigned; that one identity can hold multiple role assignments, but you cannot attach both types or several user-assigned identities to the same assignment.

domanda: A new administrator is being onboarded to Azure Policy. Select the correct answer for each drop-down to complete the onboarding cheat sheet.
opzione_a: Scopes at which a policy definition can be stored: [Management group or subscription | Subscription or resource group | Resource group or individual resource]
opzione_b: Assignment property used to exclude a child scope from evaluation: [notScopes | exemptionCategory | resourceSelectors]
opzione_c: Compliance state reported for a resource covered by a policy exemption: [Compliant | Exempted | Non-compliant]
opzione_d: Effect that blocks a non-compliant resource creation request: [Audit | Deny | Append]
spiegazione: A policy definition can be saved in either a management group or a subscription; those are the only two definition locations. Resource groups and individual resources are assignment scopes, not definition locations, so the other two choices are wrong. notScopes is the array property on the assignment object that determines what to exclude from evaluation; exemptionCategory is wrong because it belongs to a separate policyExemptions object and only classifies an exemption as Waiver or Mitigated, and resourceSelectors is wrong because it narrows evaluation by resource location or type for safe deployment practices rather than excluding a named scope. Exempted is the state shown for exempted resources - this is the defining benefit of an exemption over an exclusion, since the resource is still tracked in compliance reports rather than disappearing from them; Compliant would misrepresent the resource, and Non-compliant is the state the exemption is specifically meant to override. Deny is the effect that blocks the create or update request: Audit only logs the non-compliance and marks the resource, and Append alters the request by adding fields rather than blocking it (though it does fall back to deny behaviour if it would overwrite a conflicting value in the request).

domanda:
Contoso assigns a custom initiative that contains policy definitions using the deployIfNotExists, modify, and append effects to a management group. The assignment was created through the Azure portal with a system-assigned managed identity, and its enforcementMode property is set to DoNotEnforce. Evaluate each of the following statements and indicate whether it is correct.
1. A remediation task can be started for the deployIfNotExists policies in this assignment even though enforcementMode is set to DoNotEnforce.
2. The append policy in the initiative can bring existing non-compliant resources into a compliant state through a remediation task.
3. The assignment can be associated with both its current system-assigned managed identity and an additional user-assigned managed identity.
opzione_a: A remediation task can be started for the deployIfNotExists policies in this assignment even though enforcementMode is set to DoNotEnforce.
opzione_b: The append policy in the initiative can bring existing non-compliant resources into a compliant state through a remediation task.
opzione_c: The assignment can be associated with both its current system-assigned managed identity and an additional user-assigned managed identity.
spiegazione: Statement 1 is Yes: Microsoft documents explicitly that remediation tasks can be started for deployIfNotExists policies even when enforcementMode is set to DoNotEnforce. DoNotEnforce suppresses the effect during resource creation or update and suppresses Activity log entries, but evaluation still runs, compliance is still reported, and manual remediation remains available. Statement 2 is No: remediation is available only for the deployIfNotExists and modify effects. When an append policy runs during an evaluation cycle it makes no changes to resources that already exist - it only marks any resource meeting the if condition as non-compliant. This is precisely why Microsoft recommends modify over append when you need to remediate existing resources. Statement 3 is No: each Azure Policy assignment can be associated with only one managed identity, which is either system-assigned or user-assigned. That single identity can be granted multiple roles if the initiative's definitions require several, but a second identity of any type cannot be attached to the same assignment.

domanda: Several policy assignments in Resource Manager mode apply to a single subscription. A user submits a request to create a resource. Drag the policy effects into the order in which Azure Policy evaluates them for that request, from first evaluated to last evaluated.
spiegazione: The documented order of evaluation for a Resource Manager mode request is: Disabled is checked first, to determine whether the policy rule should be evaluated at all. Append and Modify are evaluated next, because either can alter the request, and a change they make might prevent an audit or deny effect from triggering afterwards - these two effects are available only in Resource Manager mode. Deny is then evaluated; evaluating deny before audit prevents double logging of an undesired resource. Audit is evaluated next (Manual would follow it, and DenyAction is evaluated last of all). AuditIfNotExists is evaluated after audit, because unlike audit it inspects a related child or extension resource; together with deployIfNotExists it runs only after the Resource Provider returns a success code, to determine whether more compliance logging or action is required. A common error is placing Deny first on the assumption that Azure Policy blocks bad requests before doing anything else - in fact Append and Modify run first and may make the request compliant, so Deny never fires.
tags: azure policy,effects,order of evaluation,resource manager mode
